1: # Conservation of energy for a sphere-valued wave map
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Lawrence C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, second edition,
6: Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, AMS, 2010, section 12.6, exercise 14,
7: printed page 694. The preceding exercise 13 defines the sphere-valued
8: wave map. ISBN: 978-0-8218-4974-3.
9: 
10: > 14. Prove that if \(\mathbf u\) is a wave map into the unit sphere,
11: > with compact support in space, we have conservation of energy:
12: > \[
13: > \frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
14: >       |\mathbf u_t|^2+|D\mathbf u|^2\,dx=0.
15: > \]
16: 
17: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
18: 
19: A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
20: the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
21: of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
22: This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
23: correction.
24: 
25: Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
26: \(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
27: Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:
28: 
29: 1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
30: 2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
31:    \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
32:    \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
33:    assumed.
34: 3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
35:    \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
36:    \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).
37: 
38: With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define
39: 
40: \[
41: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
42: \qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
43: \]
44: 
45: The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
46: \(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
47: Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
48: and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
49: 
50: ## Fixed natural-language proof
51: 
52: ### 1. Tangency and the wave-map equation
53: 
54: Differentiate \(u\cdot u=1\) in time. The product rule gives
55: \(2u\cdot u_t=0\), so
56: 
57: \[
58: u\cdot u_t=0,\qquad
59: u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)=a(u_t\cdot u)=0.          \tag{1}
60: \]
61: 
62: No derivative of \(a\) is needed. The familiar explicit equation also
63: follows from the assumptions: twice differentiating the unit constraint
64: gives \(u\cdot u_{tt}=-|u_t|^2\) and
65: \(u\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u=-|\partial_{x_j}u|^2\).
66: Dotting the normality equation with \(u\), using \(|u|^2=1\), yields
67: \(a=\sum_j|\partial_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2\). This is a consequence,
68: not an additional PDE assumption.
69: 
70: ### 2. Common compact support and integrability
71: 
72: Fix \(t_0>0\), put \(J=[t_0/2,3t_0/2]\), and choose its compact
73: spatial set \(C\) from assumption 3. Since \(C\) is bounded, choose
74: \(R>0\) with \(C\subset(-R,R)^n\) and set \(Q=[-R,R]^n\).
75: The box has finite Lebesgue measure \((2R)^n\).
76: 
77: On the open set \((\mathbb R^n\setminus C)\times\operatorname{int}J\),
78: the map equals the constant \(q\), so all its positive-order
79: derivatives vanish. At interior times, \(e\), \(e_t\), and the
80: derivative products used below consequently vanish outside \(C\).
81: They are continuous by smoothness; their spatial sections are measurable,
82: bounded on \(Q\), and supported there. Their absolute integrals are
83: bounded by a finite constant times \(|Q|\). This proves integrability
84: of \(e(\cdot,t_0)\) and of all later terms. Since \(t_0\) was arbitrary,
85: the energy is a finite, well-defined integral at every positive time.
86: 
87: ### 3. Differentiate the energy integral
88: 
89: The product rule and equality of mixed derivatives give
90: 
91: \[
92: e_t=2u_t\cdot u_{tt}
93:    +2\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t.           \tag{2}
94: \]
95: 
96: Choose \(\eta>0\) so that
97: \([t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\subset\operatorname{int}J\).
98: Continuity of (2) on the compact box
99: \(Q\times[t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\) gives a finite bound \(|e_t|\leq B\).
100: For \(0<|h|<\eta\), the one-variable mean value theorem at fixed
101: \(x\) therefore gives
102: 
103: \[
104: \left|\frac{e(x,t_0+h)-e(x,t_0)}h\right|
105: \leq B\mathbf1_Q(x).
106: \]
107: 
108: Outside \(Q\), both densities vanish, so the bound holds throughout
109: \(\mathbb R^n\). The right side is integrable. The difference
110: quotients converge pointwise to \(e_t(x,t_0)\). Dominated convergence
111: and linearity for these integrable functions now prove
112: 
113: \[
114: E'(t_0)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e_t(x,t_0)\,dx.            \tag{3}
115: \]
116: 
117: This establishes differentiability of the actual finite integral.
118: 
119: ### 4. Integration by parts and cancellation
120: 
121: For each spatial index \(j\), at time \(t_0\) put
122: \(g_j(x)=u_t(x,t_0)\cdot\partial_{x_j}u(x,t_0)\).
123: It is smooth and vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of \(Q\),
124: because \(C\subset\operatorname{int}Q\). The product rule gives
125: 
126: \[
127: \partial_{x_j}g_j
128: =\partial_{x_j}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_j}u
129:  +u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u.
130: \]
131: 
132: Integrate first over \(x_j\in[-R,R]\) at fixed remaining coordinates.
133: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives zero because both endpoint
134: values of \(g_j\) are zero. Fubini applies on \(Q\) because the
135: derivative and its two summands are continuous and bounded on a
136: finite-measure box. Thus \(\int_Q\partial_{x_j}g_j=0\).
137: All these terms vanish outside \(Q\), so
138: 
139: \[
140: \int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t\,dx
141: =-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx.              \tag{4}
142: \]
143: 
144: Every integral is finite by step 2. Sum (4) over the finitely many
145: spatial indices and substitute (2) into (3):
146: 
147: \[
148: \begin{aligned}
149: E'(t_0)
150: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot u_{tt}\,dx
151:  -2\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx\\
152: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)\,dx=0,
153: \end{aligned}
154: \]
155: 
156: by (1). This holds at every \(t_0>0\). Hence \(E\) is differentiable
157: with zero derivative on \((0,\infty)\), and is constant there by the
158: mean value theorem. This is conservation of energy with exactly the
159: normalization in the exercise.
160:

162:

definitions.type: family of maps ℝ^n×(0,∞)→ℝ^m indexed by j∈{1,…,n}
definitions.definition: dxu(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u(x,t), the partial derivative in the jth standard coordinate, with the total derivative convention. Further expressions ∂_{x_j}ut and ∂_{x_j}dxu(j,·,t) denote partial derivatives of the displayed functions; the latter is ∂_{x_jx_j}u.
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|²=|ut(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|dxu(j,x,t)|². Norms are Euclidean; the sum is exactly the Frobenius square |D_xu|², with no factor 1/2.
et(x,t)=e_t(x,t)=d/dr e(x,r)|_{r=t}, with the total derivative convention. Its derivative and integral properties are proved, not part of the definition.
E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx, with Lebesgue measure, for t>0. This is the finite energy integral; its use is guarded by absolute integrability of every spatial section of e.

value.text: Fix x∈ℝ^n and t>0. By H002 the time section of u has derivative ut(x,t). For applying a theorem on ℝ, extend that section by q for nonpositive times; this does not change any derivative at t>0. H004 gives u(x,r)·u(x,r)=1 for r>0. M001 with both functions equal to this section gives its squared norm derivative as ut(x,t)·u(x,t)+u(x,t)·ut(x,t)=2u(x,t)·ut(x,t). The constant function 1 has derivative zero; uniqueness of derivatives gives 2u(x,t)·ut(x,t)=0, hence u(x,t)·ut(x,t)=0.

At the same point choose a from H005. Dot utt(x,t)−lap(x,t)=a u(x,t) with ut(x,t). Bilinearity and F001 give ut(x,t)·(utt(x,t)−lap(x,t))=a(ut(x,t)·u(x,t))=0. No derivative, measurability, or globally selected version of a is used. The conclusions are independent of the witness a. Since x and t were arbitrary, both asserted orthogonality identities follow.

H002 gives continuous partial derivatives of every order on the open positive-time domain, so ut,utt,dxu are smooth. Squared Euclidean norms are finite sums of component squares, so e and its partial derivatives are smooth as well. Apply M009 at every (x,r) with r>0 to u (extended arbitrarily, say by q, outside the positive-time domain). Its C² germ is supplied by H002; over ℝ the threshold in M009 is 2. Evaluate symmetry on the time direction and each standard spatial coordinate direction to obtain ∂_r dxu(j,x,r)=∂_{x_j}ut(x,r). Apply M001 to the time sections ut with itself, and dxu(j) with itself, and add the finitely many resulting derivative formulas. The dot product is symmetric over ℝ, and |v|²=v·v, so for all x∈ℝ^n,r>0,
et(x,r)=2ut(x,r)·utt(x,r)+2Σ_{j=1}^n dxu(j,x,r)·∂_{x_j}ut(x,r).
This also proves smoothness of et. Each use of time sections on ℝ can use the extension by zero outside positive times, without changing their positive-time germs.

Fix τ>0 and put J=[τ/2,3τ/2]. The endpoints are positive and strictly ordered. H006 applied to these endpoints gives existence of a compact spatial set on which the perturbation can be supported throughout J.

Choose C from F002. Apply M010 to the identity map of Euclidean ℝ^n restricted to C. There exists a finite real bound on |x| for x∈C. Taking a positive number larger than that bound, for example one plus its maximum with zero, and using |x_j|≤|x|, gives existence of R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n. This argument also works when C is empty.

Choose R from F003 and set Q=[-R,R]^n. H001 ensures the spatial dimension is a positive finite integer. The box is compact and has Lebesgue measure (2R)^n<∞. The compact set C is closed, so (ℝ^n\C)×int J is open; u equals the constant q there by F002. Every positive-order derivative of u is zero there: at each point its germ is constant, so the defining difference quotients, and then successively all derivative germs, are zero. Consequently at each r∈int J, e,et, ut·utt, dxu(j)·∂_{x_j}ut, ut·∂_{x_j}dxu(j), and ∂_{x_j}(ut·dxu(j)) vanish outside C, for every index j. H002 and F001 give continuity of these sections (products and finite sums of continuous derivative components). Their nonzero sets thus have closures contained in the closed compact C; hence they have compact support. M003 proves their absolute integrability. M010 on Q bounds each section; its absolute integral is bounded by its finite absolute bound times |Q| because it vanishes outside Q. In particular τ∈int J, so e(·,τ) is integrable. Since τ was arbitrary, this proves integrability at every positive time, together with all the asserted common-support and integrability statements and the global identities of F001.

Fix t0>0, put J=[t0/2,3t0/2], and choose C,R jointly from N002. Set Q=[-R,R]^n and η=t0/4. Then [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J. By N002, et is continuous. The product Q×[t0−η,t0+η] is compact. M010 applied to et on this product gives a finite absolute bound; replacing it by its maximum with zero gives a nonnegative such bound.

Choose B from F001 and define Vh as declared. Define χQ(x)=1 when x∈Q and χQ(x)=0 otherwise. For every 0<|h|<η and x∈Q apply M006 to the time section of e, on the interval from min(t0,t0+h) to max(t0,t0+h), with derivative et and bound B, evaluating at the upper endpoint. All times in this interval lie in [t0−η,t0+η]. This gives |e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0)|≤B|h|, also for negative h by symmetry of absolute value. For x∉Q, N002 gives e(x,t0+h)=e(x,t0)=0. Hence throughout ℝ^n, |Vh(h,x)|≤B χQ(x). Each valid quotient is a continuous compactly supported spatial function by N002 and is integrable by linearity from integrability of the two density sections. For each x, differentiability of e in time from N002 gives Vh(h,x)→et(x,t0) as h→0 through h≠0.

The measurable nonnegative function x↦B χQ(x) is integrable: its absolute integral is B|Q|=B(2R)^n<∞, since Q is a measurable box of finite measure by N002. Use M002 with increment filter h→0, h≠0, the real-valued functions Vh(h,·), limit et(·,t0), and this majorant. This punctured real neighborhood filter is countably generated (the punctured intervals of radii 1/k, k positive integer, form a countable base). F002 supplies eventual measurability, the eventual bound, and pointwise, hence almost everywhere, convergence. We obtain lim_{h→0,h≠0}∫ Vh(h,x) dx=∫ et(x,t0) dx.

For 0<|h|<η, the two density sections are integrable by N002, t0+h>0, and integral linearity gives ∫Vh(h,x) dx=(E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. Combining this identity with F003 is exactly the difference-quotient definition of differentiability at t0 and gives E'(t0)=∫et(x,t0) dx. The limit is finite because et(·,t0) is integrable by N002. As t0>0 was arbitrary, the differentiability and integral derivative formula hold for every positive time.

Fix t0>0 and 1≤j≤n. Choose C,R from N002 for τ=t0 and put Q=[-R,R]^n. Define g(x)=ut(x,t0)·dxu(j,x,t0) and d(x)=∂_{x_j}g(x). H002 makes g smooth. Apply M001 to the j-coordinate sections of its two factors. The product rule gives, for every x∈ℝ^n,
d(x)=∂_{x_j}ut(x,t0)·dxu(j,x,t0)+ut(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}dxu(j,x,t0).
N002 shows g and d vanish outside C, so they vanish on a neighborhood of the boundary of Q: the complement of the closed set C is an open set containing that boundary. The functions g,d and the two displayed summands are continuous with compact support; d and the summands are integrable by N002, and M003 also gives integrability of g.

Set k=n−1; n=k+1 by H001. Identify ℝ^n with its n real coordinates and define I(y,z) by insertion of y in position j with all remaining coordinates z kept in their original order. Its inverse takes the jth coordinate and the ordered list of other coordinates; these formulas are inverse by inspection coordinate by coordinate. With zero-based indexing i₀=j−1, this inverse is exactly piFinSuccAbove in M011, with all component spaces ℝ. M011 says it preserves product Lebesgue measure, and so does its inverse I. Set Qrest=[-R,R]^k; then I maps [-R,R]×Qrest exactly onto Q. Apply M012 with μ the restriction of real Lebesgue measure to [-R,R], ν the restriction of Lebesgue measure on ℝ^k to Qrest, and integrand (y,z)↦d(I(y,z)). It is continuous and bounded on this compact product and the product measure is finite, hence integrable; equivalently it is the restriction of the integrable compactly supported function d∘I. Change of variables under the measure-preserving coordinate equivalence therefore yields
∫_Q d(x) dx=∫_{Qrest}(∫_{[-R,R]}d(I(y,z)) dy) dz.
For k=0, ℝ^0 is the singleton of empty coordinate lists, whose product volume is one; this formula remains valid.

For every fixed z∈Qrest, the smooth real function y↦g(I(y,z)) has derivative y↦d(I(y,z)); varying y varies just coordinate j at unit speed. That derivative is continuous, and zero for |y|>R because d is zero outside C⊂int Q. Thus it has compact support in [-R,R], and M003 gives its integrability on ℝ, hence interval integrability on [-R,R]. Apply M007 with endpoints −R,R. Both endpoint values of g(I(±R,z)) are zero by F001, because these points are on the boundary of Q. Hence the interval integral of d(I(y,z)) is zero. The oriented integral from −R to R equals the integral on the closed interval [-R,R], since R>0 and singleton endpoints have Lebesgue measure zero. F002 now gives ∫_Q d=0. Since d is zero outside Q, its integral over ℝ^n is also zero.

Integrate the product formula in F001 and use F003. Its summands are integrable, so linearity gives 0=∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}ut(x,t0)·dxu(j,x,t0) dx+∫_{ℝ^n}ut(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}dxu(j,x,t0) dx. Symmetry of the real dot product and rearrangement give precisely ∫dxu(j,x,t0)·∂_{x_j}ut(x,t0) dx=−∫ut(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}dxu(j,x,t0) dx. Absolute integrability is part of F001. Arbitrary t0,j give the stated integration-by-parts identity for every positive time and every spatial index.

Fix t0>0. N002 proves integrability of e and of every term below; N003 gives differentiability of the actual finite integral and its derivative ∫et. Substitute the density derivative formula from N002 and sum the integration-by-parts identities of N004 over the finitely many j:
E'(t0)=2∫_{ℝ^n}ut(x,t0)·utt(x,t0) dx+2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}dxu(j,x,t0)·∂_{x_j}ut(x,t0) dx
=2∫_{ℝ^n}ut(x,t0)·utt(x,t0) dx−2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}ut(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}dxu(j,x,t0) dx
=2∫_{ℝ^n}ut(x,t0)·(utt(x,t0)−lap(x,t0)) dx=0.
The second equality uses N004, the third finite-sum integral linearity and the definition of the componentwise Laplacian, and the last the pointwise zero identity of N001. All integrals are finite, so these applications of linearity are legitimate. Since t0 was arbitrary, e(·,t) is integrable and E is differentiable with E'(t)=0 at every t>0.

Let s,t be arbitrary real numbers and temporarily assume L1: 0<s<t. Apply M006 to E (extended by zero outside positive times), f₁=0, on [s,t], with L=0 and y=t. F001 gives the ordinary zero derivative at every point of this entire positive-time interval, hence the derivative within the interval. The derivative bound is |0|≤0. Therefore |E(t)−E(s)|≤0(t−s)=0, and E(t)=E(s). Discharge L1 to obtain this assertion for every 0<s<t. Equal positive times give equality reflexively, and reversing two unequal positive times gives the remaining order by symmetry. Thus E(s)=E(t) for all s,t>0. Together with F001 this is P, with exactly the original energy normalization and no assertion at time zero.

value.N002: The functions ut,utt,dxu,e,et are smooth on their stated positive-time domains. For every x∈ℝ^n and r>0, et(x,r)=2ut(x,r)·utt(x,r)+2Σ_{j=1}^n dxu(j,x,r)·∂_{x_j}ut(x,r), and ∂_r dxu(j,x,r)=∂_{x_j}ut(x,r) for each 1≤j≤n. For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable. On (ℝ^n\C)×int J all positive-order derivatives of u vanish. For every r∈int J, the spatial sections of e,et, ut·utt, dxu(j,·,r)·∂_{x_j}ut, ut·∂_{x_j}dxu(j,·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(ut·dxu(j,·,r)), for each 1≤j≤n, are continuous, bounded on Q, zero outside C, and absolutely Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n.
value.N003: For every t>0 the finite energy integral E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}et(x,t) dx.
value.N004: For every t>0 and 1≤j≤n, ∫_{ℝ^n}dxu(j,x,t)·∂_{x_j}ut(x,t) dx = −∫_{ℝ^n}ut(x,t)·∂_{x_j}dxu(j,x,t) dx. Both integrals are absolutely integrable.
value.P: For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n. The finite integral E is differentiable on (0,∞), and for every t>0, E'(t)=0. For every s,t>0, E(s)=E(t).

import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators Topology
open MeasureTheory

namespace WM
abbrev X (n : ℕ) := Fin n → ℝ
abbrev Y (m : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)
def dom (n : ℕ) : Set (X n × ℝ) := {p | 0 < p.2}
noncomputable def dt {n : ℕ} {V : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup V] [NormedSpace ℝ V] (f : X n × ℝ → V) (x : X n) (t : ℝ) : V := deriv (fun r => f (x,r)) t
noncomputable def dx {n : ℕ} {V : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup V] [NormedSpace ℝ V] (f : X n × ℝ → V) (j : Fin n) (x : X n) (t : ℝ) : V := fderiv ℝ (fun y => f (y,t)) x (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def ut {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → Y m) : X n × ℝ → Y m := fun p => dt u p.1 p.2
noncomputable def utt {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → Y m) : X n × ℝ → Y m := fun p => dt (ut u) p.1 p.2

artifact.representation: PENDING_AUDIT_B. X n is the real coordinate space Fin n → ℝ, with its standard finite product Lebesgue volume. Its library sup norm is only an auxiliary coordinate topology: it has the same topology and derivative calculus as Euclidean ℝ^n; no spatial-vector norm occurs in the energy. Y m carries the Euclidean inner product and norm. Fin n indexes the original n coordinates with a zero-based relabeling. u is a total extension to all real times; H002 is smoothness only on the open set t>0, and all physical hypotheses and conclusions are restricted to t>0. Any original u extends by q at nonpositive times; conversely restriction recovers the original map. Germ-local derivatives at positive times and energy there are independent of the extension. dx is the spatial Fréchet derivative applied to the standard coordinate vector, dt the ordinary time derivative. On the smooth open domain these are the usual partial derivatives. All norms of derivatives in e are Euclidean target norms, hence its finite sum is precisely the Frobenius square, without a half. lap is the sum of the unmixed second spatial partials. The propositions regular, geometry, good, localData, supportAndRegularity and fluxData are transparent bundles of obligations, not assumptions or proved facts. Bochner Integrable for real sections means absolute Lebesgue integrability; the total integral definition is only used as finite energy after T004. For the one actual coordinate split in Fubini, T010 explicitly checks the insertion map's measure preservation, box image, and integral conversion; this stays in finite product coordinates, including the zero-dimensional remainder.
